strengths: Well-motivated problem analysis: Clear identification and articulation of why point-based drag methods fail on DiTs due to feature granularity differences, well-illustrated in Figure 2
Comprehensive technical approach: Addresses multiple challenges (region supervision, background preservation, subject consistency) with well-justified solutions
Thorough experimental validation: Extensive comparison against 9 baselines, evaluation on 2 benchmarks, multiple metrics, and ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Strong and consistent empirical results: Achieves best or competitive performance across all metrics on both DragBench-DR and ReD Bench with impressive qualitative results
New benchmark contribution: ReD Bench provides valuable region-level annotations with task tags and detailed descriptions, advancing evaluation methodology
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, clear hyperparameter specifications, promise to release code/datasets, comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: Region-based affine supervision is relatively straightforward; hard constraints are intuitive; adapter injection leverages existing IP-Adapter; MLLM task disambiguation is orthogonal. The contribution is primarily a combination and application rather than fundamental innovation

Narrow model-specific design: Method is specifically optimized for FLUX.1-dev; generalization to other DiTs is unclear. No evaluation on SD models or other DiT architectures to demonstrate broader applicability

Unresolved CFG-distillation limitation: Paper acknowledges but works around FLUX's inversion drift rather than solving it. IFbg ranks second due to inherent model limitations, suggesting adaptation to weakness rather than capability advancement

Incomplete baseline comparison: Most comparable baseline is RegionDrag (also region-based), but no experiment with RegionDrag using FLUX as base model. Unclear how much improvement comes from method vs. base model upgrade
User input burden underexplored: Both DragFlow and RegionDrag require manual source region specification; practical advantage over RegionDrag unclear. User study would strengthen usability claims
Missing computational analysis: No runtime comparison with baselines; unclear if 70 optimization iterations is practical for interactive editing; overhead of reconstruction branch not quantified
Insufficient failure analysis: Acknowledges 'detail loss in highly intricate structures' but provides no examples, quantitative analysis, or boundary case discussion
Evaluation metric limitations: Heavy reliance on LPIPS which has known limitations; no user study validation; no analysis of metric correlation with human preference
Orthogonal MLLM contribution: Task disambiguation via GPT-5 could be applied to other methods; contribution to results unclear; adds external dependency
ReD Bench scale: 120 images is relatively small for a benchmark; no inter-rater agreement analysis for annotations

strengths: Clear problem identification with well-visualized analysis of why point-based methods fail on DiTs (Section 3.1, Fig. 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two benchmarks with nine baselines and detailed ablations
Consistent empirical improvements in Mean Distance metrics across benchmarks
Thorough documentation with extensive implementation details and dataset specifications
Practical framework that achieves visually convincing results on challenging editing scenarios
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (region supervision, gradient masking, adapters) without novel methodology; primarily an engineering adaptation rather than conceptual contribution
Insufficient differentiation from RegionDrag (Lu et al., 2024a); missing direct comparison on same FLUX backbone to isolate novel contributions
Problematic MLLM dependency on GPT-5 without ablation; raises reproducibility, cost, and latency concerns; treated as essential but not rigorously evaluated
Small benchmark: ReD Bench contains only 120 images; modified MD2 metric (centroid-based vs. point-based) makes comparison with other works difficult
No human perceptual evaluation studies to validate claimed improvements in 'faithfulness' and 'quality' over baselines
Adapter-enhanced inversion treats symptoms (CFG distillation drift) rather than root causes; only tested with InstantCharacter without exploring alternatives
Incomplete ablations: no evaluation of MLLM component, missing layer selection justification beyond empirical PCA inspection, limited scope to only FLUX variant
Ranks second on IFbg metric despite background preservation claims; hard constraint approach requires additional reconstruction branch with unquantified overhead
Methodological concerns: linear schedule (k/K) for affine transformations lacks justification; hard vs. soft constraint trade-offs unexplored

Presentation issues: unclear central contribution (region supervision, DiT adaptation, or technique combination?); overstated claims ('unleashing DiT priors'); critical details scattered across 30+ pages

strengths: Clear problem identification with well-motivated analysis of why point-based drag editing fails on DiTs (Section 3.1, Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablations (Table 3), evaluation on two benchmarks, and extensive qualitative comparisons with 9 baselines
Well-designed practical system with adaptive components (MLLM intent inference, adaptive masking, multi-operation weighting)
Introduction of ReD Bench, a new region-based dragging benchmark with point-to-region alignment and explicit task annotations
Excellent presentation with clear writing, detailed implementation information, and good reproducibility specifications
Strong quantitative results demonstrating lowest Mean Distance across both ReD Bench and DragBench-DR
Principled solution to CFG-distilled model limitations through hard constraint background preservation (Eq. 4)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: region-level supervision via affine transformations is conceptually straightforward; hard constraints and adapter-enhanced inversion are borrowed from prior work with minimal adaptation

Significant reproducibility concern: paper claims MLLM used only for 'text polishing' but Figure 3 shows MLLM as core to task interpretation and requires proprietary GPT-5, contradicting accessibility claims
Benchmark limitations: ReD Bench is small (120 images), author-created without third-party validation, and may have implicit bias toward proposed method
Limited generalization: method heavily specialized to FLUX with CFG distillation; feature layer selection (blocks 17-18) is manual; unclear how to adapt to future DiT variants
Incomplete baseline comparisons: most baselines optimized for SD not FLUX; limited region-based comparisons; unclear how much improvement comes from stronger base model vs. proposed method
Missing failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes, failure cases, or problem image types despite mentioning issues with intricate structures
Insufficient evaluation: no computational cost analysis, timing comparisons, user studies, or sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters (learning rates, iteration counts, k/K schedule)
Background preservation trade-off: ranks 2nd on IFbg metric; fundamental CFG distillation drift limitations remain partially unresolved
Unclear hyperparameter justification: choice of learning rates (1000/1200), iteration count (70), and why linear k/K schedule is optimal not ablated

strengths: Well-motivated problem analysis: Clear explanation of why point-based methods fail on DiTs due to feature granularity differences (Section 3.1, Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Two benchmarks, multiple complementary metrics, 9 baseline comparisons, thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Solid technical approach: Region-level affine supervision is sensible and well-formulated; progressive transformation strategy is elegant
Excellent reproducibility: Extensive implementation details in appendix, layer selection justification (Figure 9), hyperparameter documentation
New benchmark contribution: ReD Bench provides valuable point-to-region alignments and explicit task labels for future work
Strong qualitative results: Clear visual improvements over baselines, especially on complex scenarios with intricate details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Region-based supervision, gradient masking, and IP-Adapter integration are straightforward combinations of existing techniques; core contribution is primarily engineering for DiTs

Unfair experimental comparison: DragFlow uses FLUX (vastly larger model) while most baselines use Stable Diffusion; makes it difficult to isolate contribution of proposed techniques from architectural advantages
Computational cost prohibitive: Requires 158.7s and 23.5GB memory vs. 9.2-113.2s and 4-19GB for baselines—2-3x overhead limits practical deployment

Heavy external dependencies: Relies on MLLM (GPT-5) for prompt generation, pretrained IP-Adapter, and InstantCharacter adapter; makes method less self-contained and introduces external API costs/latency
Mixed background preservation results: Ranks second on IFbg metric despite claiming 'robust background integrity'; marginal improvement over RegionDrag (0.992 vs 1.000) contradicts claims
Input precision dependency: Method is sensitive to mask quality; undersized/incomplete masks significantly degrade results; limits practical usability
Weak benchmark: ReD Bench has only 120 images; modified MD2 metric may not be comparable to future work; affine assumption doesn't always hold for complex non-rigid deformations
MLLM dependency inelegant: Task classification via external LLM feels like workaround rather than principled solution; adds cost and latency
